taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes T. cyrtopsis was for many years called T. eques; Animal Diversity Web lists it as 'Blackneck Garter Snake'.
fieldMarks: Olive-gray to brown back, gray or bluish-gray head, whitish to greenish or brownish belly; adults 41-71 cm (rarely to 109 cm).
Yellow to white mid-dorsal stripe, shading to orange toward the head, separating two black blotches, one on each side of the neck.
Two rows of alternating dark spots between the stripes give a checkerboard look; lateral stripes (cream, tan or yellow) on scale rows 2 and 3.
19 rows of keeled dorsal scales; juveniles are brighter and more contrasting than adults.
behavior: Semi-aquatic and most active by day, though night activity is not unusual; if threatened it flees into cover or water, flattens and broadens its head, and releases foul-smelling musk.
Eats mainly frogs, toads and tadpoles, plus small fish, skinks, crustaceans and earthworms; forages actively in spring when water and prey are abundant and uses sit-and-wait ambush in summer.
At night shelters in exposed roots along stream banks, crevices, rodent holes and debris; hibernates in winter dens.
habitat: Streams in valleys and canyons and shallow rocky pools, also riparian woodland, pine-oak forest, scrub, desert flats and dry grassland; may use cattle tanks as water recedes.
range: Southern Colorado, southwestern Utah, central and eastern Arizona, New Mexico (except the far east) and western and central Texas, south through Mexico to Guatemala. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Checkered gartersnake (Thamnophis marcianus)
lookalikes.howToTell: Checkered gartersnake has 21 rows of keeled dorsal scales, a pale-yellow crescent behind the head and a single thick black neck line, versus 19 rows and two black neck blotches in the black-necked.
